twinkle.name: Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star
twinkle.tip: The melody comes from the French song “Ah! vous dirai-je, maman,” on which Mozart wrote a set of 12 variations.

silent.name: Silent Night
silent.tip: First sung in 1818 in the Austrian town of Oberndorf. The church organ is said to have broken down, so the premiere was accompanied on guitar instead.

green.name: Greensleeves
green.tip: Often said to have been written by King Henry VIII, but the tune only appeared after his death, so that is most likely just a legend.

grace.name: Amazing Grace
grace.tip: Its lyricist, John Newton, was once the captain of a slave ship. He later became a minister and supported the abolition of the slave trade.

auld.name: Auld Lang Syne
auld.tip: The words are by the Scottish poet Robert Burns. “Auld Lang Syne” means “long, long ago,” and in many places it is sung together at New Year.

prelude.name: Prelude in C Major
prelude.tip: The first piece in Book I of Bach’s The Well-Tempered Clavier. Gounod later added a melody on top of it, creating his famous “Ave Maria.”

air.name: Air on the G String
air.tip: From Bach’s Orchestral Suite No. 3. “Air on the G String” comes from a 19th-century arrangement by violinist August Wilhelmj, played on the G string alone.

canon.name: Canon in D
canon.tip: The original is a Canon and Gigue for three violins and continuo. The eight notes of the bass line repeat 28 times from beginning to end.

minuetg.name: Minuet in G Major
minuetg.tip: Long thought to be by Bach; only in the 1970s was Petzold confirmed as the composer. It appears in the notebook Bach compiled for his wife.

hallelujah.name: Hallelujah Chorus
hallelujah.tip: From the oratorio Messiah. Legend has it that King George II stood up when he heard this chorus, and audiences have stood to listen ever since.

spring.name: Spring (The Four Seasons)
spring.tip: Each concerto of The Four Seasons is paired with a sonnet. The score of “Spring” is marked with birdsong, flowing streams and thunderstorms.

fireworks.name: Fireworks: La Réjouissance
fireworks.tip: Written in 1749 for London’s peace-treaty fireworks celebration. The public rehearsal before the official performance reportedly drew over 10,000 people.

beet7.name: Symphony No. 7, 2nd Mvt.
beet7.tip: At its 1813 premiere the second movement was so popular the audience demanded an instant encore. Wagner called the symphony “the apotheosis of the dance.”

pathetique2.name: Pathétique Sonata, 2nd Mvt.
pathetique2.tip: “Pathétique” was reportedly the publisher’s title, approved by Beethoven. Billy Joel borrowed this melody for the chorus of “This Night.”

ode.name: Ode to Joy
ode.tip: From the Ninth Symphony’s finale, with words from Schiller’s poem. Beethoven was nearly deaf at the premiere. It is now also the European Union’s anthem.

k545.name: Sonata K. 545
k545.tip: Mozart himself described it in his catalogue as “a little sonata for beginners,” and it is still a must-play piece for piano students.

nacht.name: Eine kleine Nachtmusik
nacht.tip: The German title means “a little serenade.” Mozart never published it in his lifetime; it appeared only more than thirty years after his death.

elise.name: Für Elise
elise.tip: The manuscript was not discovered until the 1860s. Who “Elise” was remains unsettled, and some think the name was a miscopying of “Therese.”

fifth.name: Symphony No. 5
fifth.tip: The opening four notes, three short and one long, are world famous. Beethoven reportedly called it “fate knocking at the door,” but this is disputed.

turkish.name: Turkish March
turkish.tip: The third movement of Mozart’s Piano Sonata in A major, K. 331, it imitates the Turkish military bands that were fashionable in Europe at the time.

moon.name: Moonlight Sonata
moon.tip: Beethoven only called it a “sonata in the manner of a fantasy.” After his death a critic likened the first movement to moonlight on a lake: “Moonlight.”

lullaby.name: Lullaby (Wiegenlied)
lullaby.tip: Brahms wrote it for the birth of friend Bertha Faber’s second son. The first verse comes from the German folk-song collection Des Knaben Wunderhorn.

fantaisie.name: Fantaisie-Impromptu (Theme)
fantaisie.tip: Chopin did not want this piece published during his lifetime. It was edited and issued after his death by his friend Fontana.

raindrop.name: Raindrop Prelude
raindrop.tip: Reportedly written while Chopin recovered on Majorca, listening to rain dripping from the eaves. The repeated single note sounds like raindrops.

danube.name: The Blue Danube
danube.tip: The 1867 premiere was a choral version with a modest response. Reworked for orchestra, it swept the world; now a regular Vienna New Year’s Concert encore.

wedding.name: Wedding March
wedding.tip: Mendelssohn wrote it as incidental music for A Midsummer Night’s Dream. It became a wedding staple after the 1858 wedding of Britain’s Princess Victoria.

nocturne.name: Nocturne Op. 9 No. 2
nocturne.tip: The nocturne as a piano piece was invented by the Irish composer Field. Chopin made it famous, and Op. 9 No. 2 is the best known of them.

traum.name: Träumerei
traum.tip: Taken from Schumann’s Kinderszenen (Scenes from Childhood), one of 13 short piano pieces written for adults to look back on their childhood.

schubert.name: Ave Maria (Schubert)
schubert.tip: Originally a song set to Scott’s long poem The Lady of the Lake. Its text begins with “Ave Maria,” so it was later sung with the Latin prayer instead.

gounod.name: Ave Maria (Gounod)
gounod.tip: Gounod used Bach’s Prelude in C major as the accompaniment, wrote a new melody over it, and then set it to the Latin prayer.

anitra.name: Anitra’s Dance
anitra.tip: From Grieg’s incidental music for Ibsen’s play Peer Gynt. It is the dance Anitra performs for Peer Gynt.

minute.name: Minute Waltz
minute.tip: Reportedly written after Chopin watched George Sand’s little dog chase its tail in circles. In “Minute Waltz,” “minute” means “small,” not “sixty seconds.”

homesweet.name: Home, Sweet Home
homesweet.tip: From the 1823 opera Clari. Its famous line, “there’s no place like home,” comes from this song.

loreley.name: Die Loreley
loreley.tip: Words by Heine: a siren on a Rhine rock lures boatmen onto the rocks with her singing. The Loreley rock really exists on the Rhine.

lastrose.name: The Last Rose of Summer
lastrose.composer: Irish traditional melody (words by Thomas Moore, arr. Stevenson, 1813)
lastrose.tip: The words are by the Irish poet Moore. Flotow worked it into his opera Martha, and Mendelssohn also wrote a fantasy on it.

queennight.name: Queen of the Night Aria
queennight.tip: From The Magic Flute, premiered in 1791. The Queen of the Night must sing all the way up to a high F, making this one of the most difficult soprano arias.

brindisi.name: Brindisi (La Traviata)
brindisi.tip: From Act I of Verdi’s opera La Traviata, sung by the male lead with raised glass at a party. “Brindisi” simply means a drinking toast.

gymno.name: Gymnopédie No. 1
gymno.tip: “Gymnopédie” was a title Satie coined himself, perhaps inspired by ancient Greek dance festivals. Debussy later orchestrated two of the set.

clair.name: Clair de Lune
clair.tip: From Debussy’s Suite bergamasque. The title is taken from the poem “Clair de lune” by the French poet Verlaine.

stripesfor.name: Stars and Stripes Forever
stripesfor.tip: Sousa was known as the “March King.” In 1987 this march was designated the national march of the United States.

entertainer.name: The Entertainer
entertainer.tip: Joplin was known as the “King of Ragtime.” This piece became popular again after it was used in the 1973 film The Sting.

mountain.name: Hall of the Mountain King
mountain.tip: Also from the Peer Gynt music. The melody starts low and slow, then grows faster and louder, depicting Peer Gynt being chased by trolls.

carmen.name: Carmen Prelude
carmen.tip: Carmen was poorly received at its 1875 premiere, and Bizet died three months later, never seeing it become one of the most popular operas.

mapleleaf.name: Maple Leaf Rag
mapleleaf.tip: After its publication in 1899 sales grew year after year, and it became Joplin’s best-selling work. The title is said to come from the Maple Leaf Club.

harkherald.name: Hark! The Herald Angels Sing
harkherald.tip: The melody comes from a chorus Mendelssohn wrote to commemorate Gutenberg, the inventor of printing. He himself said it would not suit sacred words.

firstnoel.name: The First Noel
firstnoel.tip: “Noel” is the French word for Christmas. The words of this traditional English carol were first printed in 1823, and the tune was not published until 1833.

restyemerry.name: God Rest Ye Merry, Gentlemen
restyemerry.tip: In Dickens’s A Christmas Carol, Scrooge frightens off a boy who sings this carol at his door. “Rest you merry” means “may you be well.”

deck.name: Deck the Halls
deck.tip: The tune is the 16th-century Welsh New Year song “Nos Galan.” The English words were added only in the 19th century.

jingle.name: Jingle Bells
jingle.tip: Originally titled “One Horse Open Sleigh,” and its words do not mention Christmas. In 1965 astronauts played it on a harmonica aboard Gemini 6.

holynight.name: O Holy Night
holynight.tip: Written by the French composer Adam, who also composed the ballet Giselle. The words were originally a French poem.

wishmerry.name: We Wish You a Merry Christmas
wishmerry.tip: A traditional song from the west of England. The “figgy pudding” in the lyrics is the treat that carolers ask the householder for.

joyworld.name: Joy to the World
joyworld.tip: Watts wrote the words from Psalm 98; originally not a Christmas carol. The tune is credited to Handel but was mostly arranged by Mason.

nearermygod.name: Nearer, My God, to Thee
nearermygod.tip: Legend has it that this hymn was the last piece played by the band as the Titanic sank.

abidewithme.name: Abide with Me
abidewithme.tip: The Rev. Lyte wrote the poem in the weeks before his death from illness. It is still sung by the whole crowd before the FA Cup Final in England.

adeste.name: O Come, All Ye Faithful
adeste.tip: The Latin title Adeste Fideles means “Come, you faithful.” The work is usually credited to the 18th-century Englishman Wade.

littletown.name: O Little Town of Bethlehem
littletown.tip: The Rev. Brooks wrote the words after a trip to Bethlehem in 1865, and the organist Redner then composed the tune for the children of his Sunday school.

awayinmanger.name: Away in a Manger
awayinmanger.tip: Long thought to have been written by Martin Luther, but the words in fact first appeared in 19th-century America.

friendjesus.name: What a Friend We Have in Jesus
friendjesus.tip: Scriven wrote the poem to comfort his mother, who was far away at home, and never intended to publish it.

angelshigh.name: Angels We Have Heard on High
angelshigh.tip: The refrain “Gloria in excelsis Deo” is Latin for “Glory to God in the highest,” and the single syllable “Glo” is stretched over a long run of notes.

mollymalone.name: Molly Malone
mollymalone.tip: The Molly of the song is a young woman who sells seafood from a cart on the streets of Dublin, and a bronze statue of her stands in central Dublin.

london.name: London Bridge
london.tip: London Bridge has been damaged and rebuilt many times. In the 1960s an American bought an old London Bridge and had it moved and rebuilt in Arizona.

rowboat.name: Row, Row, Row Your Boat
rowboat.tip: This is a round: several people start from the beginning at staggered times, and the melodies layer into harmony.

happybday.name: Happy Birthday to You
happybday.tip: The melody was originally “Good Morning to All,” written by the Hill sisters for kindergarten children, and only later got its birthday words.

jacques.name: Frère Jacques
jacques.tip: The French original asks a friar “Are you sleeping?” and tells him to ring morning bells. Mahler made it a minor-key funeral march in Symphony No. 1.

alohaoe.name: Aloha ʻOe
alohaoe.tip: Its composer, Liliʻuokalani, was the last monarch of the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi. “Aloha ʻOe” means “farewell to you.”

yankee.name: Yankee Doodle
yankee.tip: During the American Revolution, British troops mocked colonial soldiers with this song, but Americans made it a victory song. Now Connecticut’s state song.

korobeiniki.name: Korobeiniki
korobeiniki.tip: The words come from a poem by Nekrasov about a traveling peddler. Many people know the tune from the Tetris background music.

jollygood.name: He’s a Jolly Good Fellow
jollygood.tip: The tune is the same as the old French song “Malbrough s’en va-t-en guerre,” which Beethoven also used in Wellington’s Victory.

pixel.name: Pixel Jump
pixel.tip: An original PingPongLight piece with the sound of a retro video game.

velvet.name: Velvet Groove
velvet.tip: An original PingPongLight piece with a slower tempo and a soft groove.

neon.name: Neon Rush
neon.tip: An original PingPongLight piece written for fast-paced neon visuals.

scarborough.name: Scarborough Fair
scarborough.tip: An old English folk song whose lyrics ask the other person for one impossible task after another. Simon and Garfunkel’s 1966 cover spread it worldwide.

londonderry.name: Londonderry Air
londonderry.tip: Traditional tune from County Londonderry, Ireland (now Northern Ireland), in Petrie’s 1855 Irish collection. Reworded, it became the famous “Danny Boy.”

auralee.name: Aura Lee
auralee.tip: An American song published in 1861, sung by soldiers on both sides of the Civil War. In 1956 its melody got new words as Elvis Presley’s “Love Me Tender.”

shenandoah.name: Shenandoah
shenandoah.tip: A 19th-century American folk song said to have been sung first by boatmen on the Missouri River, and later by sailors as they weighed anchor.

molihua.name: Mo Li Hua (Jasmine Flower)
molihua.tip: From the Qing-dynasty Jiangnan tune “Xianhua Diao,” notated by the British and taken to Europe by the late 18th century. Puccini’s Turandot also quotes it.

arirang.name: Arirang
arirang.tip: The Korean Peninsula’s most representative folk song, with dozens of versions. In 2012 it joined UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity list.

santalucia.name: Santa Lucia
santalucia.tip: A Neapolitan boat song published by Cottrau in 1849, describing the Bay of Naples seascape at Santa Lucia; a boatman invites you out on the evening breeze.

funicula.name: Funiculì, Funiculà
funicula.tip: Written in 1880 for the Vesuvius funicular opening. Richard Strauss mistook it for folk music, used it in the symphonic fantasy Aus Italien, and was sued.

sakura.name: Sakura Sakura
sakura.tip: Traditional Japanese song, a beginner’s koto piece by the Edo period. Spread by the Tokyo Music School’s 1888 koto book; now among Japan’s signature tunes.

kalinka2.name: Kalinka
kalinka2.tip: Larionov wrote it for a play in 1860; often taken for Russian folk music. Its title is a pet name for the guelder-rose berry; speeding up is its trademark.

largo.name: Largo (New World Symphony)
largo.tip: Dvořák wrote the New World Symphony in America. Its second movement’s homesick English horn melody was later given words as the familiar “Going Home.”

salut.name: Salut d’Amour
salut.tip: Elgar’s engagement present to his fiancée Caroline Alice. The publisher changed its German title to the French “Salut d’Amour” to help it sell.

flowerwaltz.name: Waltz of the Flowers
flowerwaltz.tip: From Act II (Land of Sweets) of the 1892 ballet The Nutcracker. A harp cadenza leads in, then horns and strings share the theme; a suite favorite.

morning.name: Morning Mood (Peer Gynt)
morning.tip: Grieg wrote it for Ibsen’s dramatic poem Peer Gynt. Often imagined as a Nordic morning, it actually shows the hero greeting sunrise in the Moroccan desert.

barcarolle.name: Barcarolle (Hoffmann)
barcarolle.tip: A Venice duet from the opera The Tales of Hoffmann, its swaying 6/8 beat evoking gondolas. Offenbach died months before the premiere, never hearing it.

hungarian5.name: Hungarian Dance No. 5
hungarian5.tip: Brahms arranged Hungarian Gypsy-style tunes for piano four hands; the speeding-and-slowing No. 5 is most popular. Its theme is from Béla Kéler’s csárdás.

williamtell.name: William Tell Overture
williamtell.tip: Overture to Rossini’s last opera. Its finale, with sounding trumpets and a galloping hoof-beat, became shorthand for horse races and Western film scores.

trepak.name: Trepak (Russian Dance)
trepak.tip: The trepak is a fast Ukrainian and Russian stamping dance. Tchaikovsky put it in The Nutcracker’s Land of Sweets, speeding up and racing to a rapid close.

radetzky.name: Radetzky March
radetzky.tip: Johann Strauss I wrote it in 1848 for Field Marshal Radetzky’s victory in Italy. It always closes the Vienna New Year’s Concert, audience clapping along.

cancan.name: Can-Can
cancan.tip: From Offenbach’s operetta Orpheus in the Underworld (1858), originally the “Galop infernal.” It became the signature accompaniment of the Paris can-can.

revolution.name: Revolutionary Étude
revolution.tip: Written in Stuttgart in 1831 on news that the November Uprising had failed. The racing left hand sounds like anger and grief: the classic left-hand étude.

bumblebee.name: Flight of the Bumblebee
bumblebee.tip: Rimsky-Korsakov’s 1900 interlude in his opera The Tale of Tsar Saltan depicts a prince turned bumblebee stinging his wicked aunts; a famous showpiece.

bwv565.name: Toccata in D Minor
bwv565.tip: The best-known organ work. Its plunging opening scale and dissonant chords stand for “horror” and “drama.” Scholars still debate whether it is Bach’s.

campanella.name: La Campanella
campanella.tip: Adapted from the finale of Paganini’s Violin Concerto No. 2 and revised by Liszt in 1851 as a grand étude. The repeated high D-sharp imitates a bell.

paganini24.name: Caprice No. 24
paganini24.tip: A pinnacle of solo violin writing, in which a short theme gives rise to 11 variations. Liszt, Brahms and Rachmaninoff have all written works based on it.
